@Wrenna Robson and @Jon Eugster, starting a thread for upstreaming Nat.Bits from Mathlib to Batteries, as discussed.

Context : I have an open Mathlib PR (#36463) that adds Nat.ofListBool (a list-based version of Nat.ofBits) and proves its injectivity. Instead of adding this to the legacy Mathlib.Data.Nat.Bits file, we decided it's better to upstream this logic to Batteries, and eventually deprecate the old Mathlib file.

Question on file structure: I see that Nat.ofBits currently lives in Batteries.Data.Nat.Basic. For this initial PR, should the new ofListBool function and its lemmas go directly into Basic.lean alongside it, or is it better to create a new dedicated file (e.g., Batteries.Data.Nat.Bits) for this and the rest of the planned refactoring?

Additions need both definitions and theorems. The definitions are best added as early as possible in existing files, the theorems can be in a separate file. Make sure the theorem file does not contain any definitions at all.

François G. Dorais said:

Additions need both definitions and theorems. The definitions are best added as early as possible in existing files, the theorems can be in a separate file. Make sure the theorem file does not contain any definitions at all.

This is the first I have heard of this. Is this special to batteries? Or is the idea that the theorems file contains no definitions applicable to new PRs also? (I was thinking of making a multi-file submission where the main theorem file also has a definition.)

content: Yes that's the general style in Batteries
My suggestion would be we start with the definitions before doing lots of theorems.
At minimum I think we should add: Nat.bit, Nat.bodd, Nat.div2 (though I wouldn't define them in the same way). We also need to decide exactly how to do the calculation of the bits.
I would argue it's very useful to have Nat.size as well as it's the length of the bits.
Nat.ofBits is tuple-based, right?

@Wrenna Robson
Yes, Nat.ofBits is tuple-based (Fin n → Bool).

I've put together a quick draft of how I understand we could define these using modern Lean 4 primitives (avoiding the old binaryRec approach).

/-- Appends a bit to the right of a natural number. -/
@[inline] def bit (b : Bool) (n : Nat) : Nat :=
2 * n + b.toNat

/-- Returns true if the natural number is odd. -/
@[inline] def bodd (n : Nat) : Bool :=
n.testBit 0 -- or n % 2 == 1 ?

/-- Divides a natural number by 2, dropping the least significant bit. -/
@[inline] def div2 (n : Nat) : Nat :=
n / 2 -- or n >>> 1 ?

/-- The number of bits required to represent a natural number. -/
@[inline] def size (n : Nat) : Nat :=
if n == 0 then 0 else n.log2 + 1

/-- Constructs a natural number from a little-endian list of bits. -/
@[inline] def ofBitsList (bs : List Bool) : Nat :=
bs.foldr bit 0

I have a few questions to make sure this fits the Batteries style:

  1. Naming: Is ofBitsList okay, or would ofListBool be better to follow a stricter of<Type> convention?

  2. Primitives: For bodd and div2, as I understand it, arithmetic ops (/ 2, % 2) are usually easier for proofs, but bitwise ops (>>> 1, testBit 0) might be faster. What is the preference here?

  3. Folding: foldr is great for the inductive proofs we'll do later, but let me know if a tail-recursive foldl is preferred for performance.

Once we agree on the basic shape, I can open the initial PR and add you as a co-author.
We would still need the way of extracting the bits, which fundamentally wants some kind of recursor.
Primitives - define using performance things. Early theorem will be showing this equivalent to the other form.
Like Nat.bits should exist fundamentally
And that imo is the harder thing to define well.
There's very clearly a recursive way of doing it using div2 and bodd but it may not be performant (but maybe we don't care.

I experimented with the recursive definition locally. I initially tried using n >>> 1 for the recursive step, but the termination checker fails in Basic.lean (it requires a proof that n >>> 1 < n, which seems to need lemmas that aren't available this early in the file hierarchy).

To keep Basic.lean clean without complex decreasing_by tactics, using the arithmetic n / 2 makes the termination trivial. Here is the addition:
@[inline] def div2 (n : Nat) : Nat :=
n / 2

/-- Extracts the bits of a natural number as a little-endian list. -/
def bits (n : Nat) : List Bool :=
if _h : n = 0 then
[]
else
bodd n :: bits (n / 2)
termination_by n

As I understand it, since Lean uses GMP for Nat under the hood, n / 2 should be optimized to a bitshift at the binary level anyway, so hopefully we aren't actually sacrificing performance here?

I added these definitions to my local Batteries.Data.Nat.Basic and a full lake build passed successfully. Does this approach look like a good compromise to you?
I am surprised we don't have the necessary at this point in the hierarchy. But yes that's basically the definition I would expect.

This duplicates parts of batteries#1293.

@François G. Dorais , please correct me if I'm wrong, but it seems to me that Nat.bits might not be a strict duplicate. While mathematically base-2 digits are indeed the same as bits, programmatically they seem to serve different needs.

#1293 generalizes digits using Fin base, whereas Nat.bits works directly with Bool. Having a dedicated Bool API allows us to natively use fast bitwise primitives (like testBit and >>>) and standard boolean logic, which is very common for CS applications.

Yes I do think it would be a mistake to say that Nat.digits replicates it, but there's clearly some overlap. If nothing else you want to closely look at the approach in both places and prove the necessary compatibility theorems.
Why aren't you using BitVec?
I just realized that my old PR #13649 was never merged...

@François G. Dorais
Let me step back and explain my original motivation for this, which hopefully clears things up.

  1. I recently developed a repository formalizing Kolmogorov Complexity, and I am currently trying to gradually upstream parts of it into Mathlib.
  2. To properly define the Kolmogorov complexity of a natural number, I fundamentally need a computable bijection (or at least an injection) between Nat and the set of all finite binary strings, with the property that a number $N$ maps to a string of length $\log_2 N + O(1)$.
  3. BitVec n is a fixed-width type. Representing the set of all finite binary strings $\{0,1\}^*$ would require a Sigma type like Σ n, BitVec n. Using dependent pairs makes structural induction and computability proofs unnecessarily painful compared to a simple List Bool.
Why don't you define Kolmogorov complexity in terms of List Bool? I think it's much more intuitive that way.
Of course, I don't know what TM model you're using.
But if your TM model uses Nat then they must have tools to interpret Nat as lists of bits in some way...

@François G. Dorais
That is exactly what I am doing! The base Kolmogorov complexity is defined strictly in terms of strings (List Bool).

However, Kolmogorov complexity can be extended to any other constructive object, such as natural numbers. For a number $N$, its complexity will have the property that it is bounded by $\log_2 N + O(1)$.

But to actually prove this upper bound in Lean, we need a computable injection from Nat to List Bool which maps $N$ to a string of length $\approx \log_2 N$. That is exactly the missing piece I am trying to build with this Nat.bits API
When you say "why aren't you using BitVec" - the issue there would be that you need to know the size of bitvector you're using!
You can define the sigma type over BitVec + a custom bitwise induction principle and then use all of the API already developed for BitVec in core.
If you think that's the better approach...
I don't understand why we'd want Nat.digits (per the above PR) but not have Nat.toBits.
I feel pretty sure there are natural applications you'd want it for.

If you want KC upper and lower bounds, then I suppose you want a computable bijection. Your proposal is incorrect since it strips trailing zeros. A correct bijection is, for example:

  • Nat -> List Bool: represent n+1 in base 2 as a list and delete the leading 1.
  • List Bool -> Nat: add a leading 1 to the list l, evaluate as a positive integer then subtract 1.
I don't understand why you want Nat.bits in Batteries. I don't mind adding it I just want to know what it is good for.
If you want a really efficient implementation of BitList then I'm afraid Sigma BitVec is just as good since that's probably how it would be implemented under the hood.
Is BitVec really that efficient?
BitVec is just a Nat with a size assumption
Well, that's why I ask.

I think there's a couple of needs in tension. There are good theoretical reasons why having the actual bit list is useful - off the top of my head it's useful when implementing XMSS. Now you might be able to do that with just fixed size stuff but I can think of technical reasons why that might be a big headache. But there's also the Kolmogorov complexity thing - maybe for that you need the bijection. That's not really my area.

BitVec does not, I believe deliberately, give you good recursor access to the bits - I don't think it's expected you use it for that. List is simply the natural thing people will reach for and it's straightforward to use. In a little bit I will be at my desk properly and I can check some stuff about definitions in core but my memory is that bitwise operators and testBit are not, like, implemented using BitVec or anything -they are primitives on Nat. I also think Nat.ofBits, which is already in Batteries, also doesn't use BitVec (or List!). So I don't really understand the rationale for what is included and what isn't there.

I don't even know if the operation that maps (n : Nat) to BitVec n.size exists - to me you'd surely want that if you did work with the Sigma type, but... calculating the size first is going to be nearly as much work as calculating the bits in the first place.

It might be the primitive you really want is a good recursor on the bits of Nat which sort of exists in MathLib, but perhaps more properly might be used to define Nat.bitwise in core. That feels like too much movement too soon to me - this proposal felt like the conservative choice.

@François G. Dorais
Yes, a proper bijection is indeed the standard approach, and it is actually what I implemented first here: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/35857

However, I later realized that for defining the Kolmogorov complexity of a natural number, a total computable injection from $\mathbb{N}$ to strings (with length $ \log n + O(1)$) works just as well.
Note that batteries#1730 exists which I think is entirely separate to the above. I disagree with the choice to upstream all the binaryRec variants here though.

Has anyone else considered this:

@[implemented_by Nat]
inductive PosNat where
| one : PosNat
| bit0 : PosNat → PosNat
| bit1 : PosNat → PosNat
deriving Inhabited

namespace PosNat

unsafe def toNatImpl (n : PosNat) : Nat := unsafeCast n

@[implemented_by toNatImpl]
opaque toNat : PosNat → Nat

unsafe def ofNatImpl (n : Nat) [NeZero n] : PosNat := unsafeCast n

@[implemented_by ofNatImpl]
opaque _root_.Nat.toPosNat (n : Nat) [NeZero n] : PosNat

unsafe def oneImpl : PosNat := unsafeCast (1 : Nat)
attribute [implemented_by oneImpl] PosNat.one

unsafe def bit0Impl (x : PosNat) : PosNat := unsafeCast <| 2 * unsafeCast x
attribute [implemented_by bit0Impl] PosNat.bit0

unsafe def bit1Impl (x : PosNat) : PosNat := unsafeCast <| 2 * unsafeCast x + 1
attribute [implemented_by bit1Impl] PosNat.bit1

A bit more is necessary to make match work but this is pretty close to optimal.

Mathlib has PosNat or something similar defined like that. They even then define a Nat variant from it. But this is solving a different problem in my view. Fundamentally bit - on Nat to Nat - is a natural function that comes up a lot.

To be honest I'm not sure why you'd do what you're doing there as opposed to other things. But essentially IMO when it comes to binary representation of Nat we have a bit of an Xkcd "there are 15 standards" issue.

At the very least I do not think you should do what you do there, but define a Nat variant from PosNat + the extra inductive bit (that's what Mathlib does) - it seems to me more correct to say that that is what Nat implements. But I do not like having implemented_by if I don't have to because it increases the trusted surface.

Compile to the obvious thing and the coercion to/from Nat and PosNat is a noop.

One of the complexities here: when a Nat is within I think 32-bits, one can use the intrinsic CLZ instruction (on architectures which have it) to calculate its bitlength very efficiently (this counts leading zeros). So clearly one can write very fast implementations of this within this range.

@Alexey Milovanov This is the way I think I would define the requisite functions - to be clear this isn't the efficient way (but that is OK because that is what csimp/implemented_by is for), but it is a nice way that doesn't mix it up with arithmetic theorems.

def bit (b : Bool) : Nat → Nat | 0 => b.toNat | n + 1 => (bit b n).succ.succ
def bodd : Nat → Bool | 0 => false  | 1 => true | n + 2 => n.bodd
def div2 : Nat → Nat  | 0 => 0      | 1 => 0    | n + 2 => n.div2.succ

Then we have:

theorem bodd_bit {b : Bool} : ∀ n : Nat, (n.bit b).bodd = b
  | 0 => b.recOn rfl rfl | n + 1 => n.bodd_bit

theorem div2_bit {b : Bool} : ∀ n : Nat, (n.bit b).div2 = n
  | 0 => b.recOn rfl rfl | n + 1 => congrArg succ n.div2_bit

theorem bit_bodd_div2 : ∀ n : Nat, n.div2.bit n.bodd = n
  | 0 | 1 => rfl | n + 2 => congrArg (succ ∘ succ) n.bit_bodd_div2

And one can show:

theorem div2_apply_eq : ∀ n : Nat, n.div2 = n / 2
  | 0 | 1 => rfl | n + 2 =>
    (congrArg succ n.div2_apply_eq).trans (Nat.add_div_right _ Nat.zero_lt_two).symm

theorem div2_eq : div2 = (· / 2) := funext div2_apply_eq

theorem bodd_apply_eq : ∀ n : Nat, n.bodd = n.testBit 0
  | 0 | 1 => rfl | n + 2 =>
    n.bodd_apply_eq.trans (n.testBit_zero ▸ (n + 2).testBit_zero ▸ (Nat.add_mod_right _ _ ▸ rfl))

theorem bodd_eq : bodd = (·.testBit 0) := funext bodd_apply_eq

theorem toNat_bodd_eq : ∀ n : Nat, n.bodd.toNat = n % 2
  | 0 | 1 => rfl | n + 2 => (toNat_bodd_eq n).trans (Nat.add_mod_right _ _).symm

theorem bit_apply_eq {b : Bool} : ∀ n, bit b n = b.toNat + 2*n
  | 0 => rfl | n + 1 => congrArg (succ ∘ succ) n.bit_apply_eq

theorem bit_eq : bit = (cond · (2 * · + 1) (2 * ·)) := funext fun b => funext
  fun n => n.bit_apply_eq.trans ((Nat.add_comm _ _).trans <| b.recOn rfl rfl)

Importantly we can show without major arithmetic lemmas:

theorem div2_lt_succ : ∀ n, n.div2 < n + 1
  | 0 => Nat.zero_lt_one | 1 => Nat.zero_lt_two | n + 2 =>
    Nat.succ_lt_succ (Nat.lt_trans n.div2_lt_succ n.succ.lt_succ_self)

And then:

@[elab_as_elim, specialize]
def binaryRecFromOne {motive : Nat → Sort u} (zero : motive 0) (one : motive 1)
    (bit : ∀ b n, n ≠ 0 → motive n → motive (bit b n)) :
    ∀ n, motive n
  | 0 => zero | 1 => one | n + 2 =>
    (n + 2).bit_bodd_div2 ▸ bit (n + 2).bodd ((n + 2).div2)
    (Nat.succ_ne_zero _) (binaryRecFromOne zero one bit _)
  termination_by n => n
  decreasing_by exact Nat.succ_lt_succ n.div2_lt_succ

def Nat.bits (n : Nat) : List Bool := n.binaryRecFromOne [] [true] (fun b _ _ bs => b :: bs)
def Nat.size (n : Nat) : Nat := n.binaryRecFromOne 0 1 (fun _ _ _ => (· + 1))

(I think this is actually my preferred form of the recursor because it's entirely structural:

@[elab_as_elim, specialize]
def binaryRecFromOne {motive : Nat → Sort u} (zero : motive 0) (one : motive 1)
    (bit : ∀ b n, motive (n + 1) → motive (bit b (n + 1))) :
    ∀ n, motive n
  | 0 => zero | 1 => one | n + 2 =>
    (n + 2).bit_bodd_div2 ▸ bit n.bodd n.div2 <| (n.div2 + 1).binaryRecFromOne zero one bit
  termination_by n => n
  decreasing_by exact Nat.succ_lt_succ n.div2_lt_succ

)

Incidentally with this recursor:

def bitsSigma (n : Nat) : (w : Nat) × (BitVec w) :=
  n.binaryRecFromOne ⟨0, 0⟩ ⟨1, 1⟩ (fun b _ H => ⟨H.1 + 1, H.2.concat b⟩)

(I honestly quite like this. But having the recursor makes it straightforward more or less, at least once you choose suitable grind lemmas)

@Wrenna Robson Thank you!

I encountered a technical issue when defining bits and size directly through binaryRecFromOne. Because the recursor has a dependent motive, it injects Eq.rec into the definitions. This blocks rfl and prevents simp from working on basic lemmas like bits (bit b (n+1)) = b :: bits (n+1).

To keep the proof API clean, I separated the computation from the induction principle. I defined bits and size directly using termination_by:

Lean

def bits : Nat → List Bool
  | 0 => []
  | 1 => [true]
  | n + 2 => bodd n :: bits (div2 n + 1)
termination_by n => n
decreasing_by exact Nat.succ_lt_succ (div2_lt_succ n)

This bypasses Eq.rec and allows the grind lemmas to be proved easily. I still use your binaryRecFromOne recursor for the induction tactic, which works perfectly for the main theorems:

Lean

theorem length_bits (n : Nat) : (bits n).length = size n := by
  induction n using binaryRecFromOne with
  | zero => simp
  | one => simp
  | step_bit b m ih => simp [ih]

I had to drop @[csimp] on div2_eq because the compiler rejected the lambda expression. What is the preferred way in Batteries to bind these structural definitions to Nat.shiftRight or an extern function for better performance?

You need two definitions: The model definition and the fast implementation. Then:

namespace Nat

def bit (b : Bool) : Nat → Nat | 0 => b.toNat | n + 1 => (bit b n).succ.succ
def bodd : Nat → Bool | 0 => false  | 1 => true | n + 2 => n.bodd
def div2 : Nat → Nat  | 0 => 0      | 1 => 0    | n + 2 => n.div2.succ

def bitImpl (b : Bool) (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  let n := 2 * n
  if b then n + 1 else n

@[inline] def boddImpl (n : Nat) : Bool := 1 &&& n == 1
@[inline] def div2Impl (n : Nat) : Nat := n >>> 1

@[csimp]
theorem bit_eq_bitImpl : bit = bitImpl := by
  funext b n; fun_induction bit <;> cases b <;> simp +arith [bitImpl, *]

@[csimp]
theorem bodd_eq_boddImpl : bodd = boddImpl := by
  funext n; fun_induction bodd <;> simp +arith [boddImpl, *]

@[csimp]
theorem div2_eq_div2Impl : div2 = div2Impl := by
  funext n; fun_induction div2 <;> simp +arith [div2Impl, Nat.shiftRight_eq_div_pow, *]
You can use the recursor for those definitions - you need some utility theorems but grind actually works with this kind of thing pretty well. I'll post it tomorrow at work.

@Wrenna Robson I got it working! Here are the grind lemmas that make everything click:

Lean

@[simp] theorem bits_bit (b : Bool) (n : Nat) : bits (bit b (n + 1)) = b :: bits (n + 1) := by
  unfold bits bit
  grind [binaryRecFromOne.eq_def, bodd_bit, div2_bit]

@[simp] theorem size_bit (b : Bool) (n : Nat) : size (bit b (n + 1)) = size (n + 1) + 1 := by
  unfold size bit
  grind [binaryRecFromOne.eq_def, bodd_bit, div2_bit]

I found this in my stash and patched it up. Big-endian but all tail-recursive. Just reverse the list for little-endian. Use as you please.

namespace Nat

/-- Calculates the natural number whose big-endian binary representation is the list `l`. -/
@[inline]
def ofBitList (l : List Bool) : Nat :=
  loop l 0
where
  loop l acc :=
    match l with
    | [] => acc
    | false :: l => loop l (2 * acc)
    | true :: l => loop l (2 * acc + 1)

theorem ofBitList.loop_eq_shiftLeft_length_add :
    loop l acc = ofBitList l + acc <<< l.length := by
  match l with
  | [] => simp [ofBitList, loop]
  | false :: l =>
    simp only [ofBitList, loop, loop_eq_shiftLeft_length_add (acc := 2 * acc), shiftLeft_eq,
      List.length_cons, Nat.pow_add_one]
    grind
  | true :: l =>
    simp only [ofBitList, loop, loop_eq_shiftLeft_length_add (acc := 2 * acc + 1),
      loop_eq_shiftLeft_length_add (acc := 1), shiftLeft_eq, List.length_cons, Nat.pow_add_one]
    grind

theorem ofBitList_append (l₁ l₂ : List Bool) :
    ofBitList (l₂ ++ l₁) = ofBitList l₂ <<< l₁.length + ofBitList l₁ := by
  simp only [ofBitList]
  induction l₂ generalizing l₁ with
  | nil => simp [ofBitList.loop]
  | cons b l₂ ih =>
    cases b
    · simp only [List.cons_append, ofBitList.loop, Nat.mul_zero, ih, shiftLeft_eq]
    · simp only [List.cons_append, ofBitList.loop, Nat.mul_zero, Nat.zero_add,
      ofBitList.loop_eq_shiftLeft_length_add (acc := 1), ofBitList, ih, shiftLeft_eq,
      List.length_append, Nat.pow_add]
      grind

/-- Calculates big-endian bit representation of the natural number `n`. -/
@[inline]
def toBitList (n : Nat) : List Bool :=
  loop n []
where
  loop n acc :=
    match n with
    | 0 => acc
    | 1 => true :: acc
    | n@(_+2) => loop (n / 2) (testBit n 0 :: acc)

@[simp] theorem toBitList.loop_zero : loop 0 acc = acc := by
  simp [loop]

@[simp] theorem toBitList.loop_one : loop 1 acc = true :: acc := by
  simp [loop]

@[simp] theorem toBitList.loop_add_two :
    loop (n+2) acc = loop ((n + 2) / 2) (testBit (n + 2) 0 :: acc) := by
  simp only [loop]

theorem toBitList.loop_eq_toBitList_append :
    loop n acc = toBitList n ++ acc := by
  match n with
  | 0 => simp [toBitList]
  | 1 => simp [toBitList]
  | n+2 =>
    simp only [loop_add_two, zero_lt_succ, add_div_right, testBit_zero, add_mod_right, toBitList]
    rw [loop_eq_toBitList_append]
    rw [loop_eq_toBitList_append]
    simp

@[simp] theorem toBitList_zero : toBitList 0 = [] := by
  simp [toBitList]

theorem toBitList_ne_zero [NeZero n] : n.toBitList = (n / 2).toBitList ++ [n.testBit 0] := by
  have := NeZero.ne n
  match n with
  | 1 => simp [toBitList]
  | n+2 =>
    simp only [toBitList, toBitList.loop_add_two, zero_lt_succ, add_div_right, testBit_zero,
      add_mod_right]
    exact toBitList.loop_eq_toBitList_append ..

#eval Nat.ofBitList (10 ^ 10000 - 11 : Nat).toBitList == 10 ^ 10000 - 11 -- almost instantaneous!
